Lessons.Title: Working with Ratios in Right Triangles
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: estimate angles and missing sides from a measured right-triangle ratio table, before introducing formal cosine, sine and tangent names.

The official student activity estimates launch angle and compares Pythagorean triples and side ratios, progressing from tables and side labels to algebraic estimates. An original hypothetical launch-slope task uses explicit units without claiming a real launch specification.

Teacher rubric (0–8): four human-scored 0/1/2 criteria cover the original launch model/angle table range, ordered ratios for source 7-24-25 triangle, two independently calculated source-known missing side lengths and source Practice with correct angle correspondence, appropriate precision and figure limitations.

First-party Edulytiks worked reasoning aligned to Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 4, CC BY 4.0. Publisher graphics, protected assessment answers and logos are not reproduced.

Source 5.1 Launch Pad (5 min): original rocket rises 50 feet for each 13 feet horizontal. Draw a RIGHT triangle with vertical rise50, horizontal run13, hypotenuse sqrt(2669) and reference launch angle about arctan(50/13)=75.43 degrees; ratio opposite/adjacent50/13 approx3.846 lies between source table70-degree2.747 and80-degree5.671. Student may first estimate 70-80 degrees and refine; do not describe this hypothetical publisher problem as real engineering specification.

Source 5.2 Pythagorean Triples (15 min): construct original source 7,24,25 right triangle, verify 7^2+24^2=25^2, label SMALLEST acute angle A opposite leg7. Three source ORDERED table ratios for A: adjacent/hyp24/25=0.96, opposite/hyp7/25=0.28, opposite/adjacent7/24 approx0.2917. Estimate small angle about16 degrees (arctan7/24) and complement about74 degrees using the previous lesson right-triangle table. Optional example 8-15-17 is another valid Pythagorean triple with angles about28 and62 degrees; label reference angle, do not substitute for original 7-24-25.

Source 5.3 Solve All the Triangles (15 min): for right triangle with angle40 degrees and OPPOSITE LEG5cm, source table opposite/hyp ratio0.643 gives hyp approximately5/0.643=7.776cm. For angle70 degrees and OPPOSITE LEG12cm, source table opposite/adjacent2.747 gives adjacent approximately12/2.747=4.368cm. The other original first and third drawings ask for segments AB and DE but accessible student text lacks the required marked side/angle values: teacher must inspect source figures rather than invent lengths. Encourage several student strategies y=kx, ratio proportion, and guess/check. Keep ratios described as adjacent/hyp, opposite/hyp and opposite/adjacent; source explicitly delays named trigonometric functions.

Source student summary first example: right triangle25-degree opposite leg5 and source opposite/adjacent ratio0.466 implies adjacent b=5/0.466 about10.73, reasonably reported10.7 units. Second example angle D from opposite/hyp0.794 and opposite/adjacent1.283 lies between source 50 row (0.766,1.192) and 60 row (0.866,1.732); estimate between50 and60 degrees, actual model about52 degrees. Values in source ratios are approximations, not exact symbolic values.

Source Practice P1-P8: P1 8,15,17 Pythagorean triple and acute angles approx28.1,61.9. P2 kite string18 feet with angle30 degrees above ground -> height9 feet assuming taut straight string and level ground. P3 right at C and hypotenuse AB10: choices D (A30,BC5) and E (AC8,BC6) correct; A,B,C wrong given their respective ratios. P4 adjacent/hyp0.45 angle about63 degrees option D. P5 reference A row0.31,0.95,3.1 -> A about72 degrees, complementary angle C about18, with reversed ratios approximately0.95,0.31,0.326 (source exact printed precision controls). P6 AB from source 30-60-90 picture depends on source figure; P7 square side from source picture depends on marked diagonal, 6/sqrt2 only if diagonal6; P8 altitude CD proportions require original figure and exact segment labels.

Source 5.4 Solve the Triangle original Cool-down is teacher login restricted. Independent Edulytiks paper alternative asks students to sketch rise/run launch, explain how two rounded reference ratios bound angle, solve the two source-known triangle side questions, and justify precision. Teacher scores reasoning and original labelled drawings; Stage D runtime test and online scoring NOT_RUN.

KeyConcepts.Title: Measured quotient
KeyConcepts.Definition: A right-triangle quotient is a ratio of named sides, such as opposite/adjacent.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Read the table row for the reference angle and choose the matching quotient.

KeyConcepts.Title: Solve from a ratio
KeyConcepts.Definition: A quotient r=opposite/hypotenuse lets you find a side if the other side is given.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Write r=o/h and solve with algebra, checking h>0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Angle estimation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Compare observed ratios with nearby rows in a table, acknowledging measured rounding.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use a bounded estimate rather than an unjustifiably exact angle.
KeyConcepts.Example: If opposite/adjacent is about 1, the acute angle is about 45°.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate a missing leg from a table
WorkedExamples.Question: A 40° right-triangle table lists opposite/hypotenuse≈0.643. Hypotenuse is 12 cm. Estimate opposite.
Steps: Round to 7.7 cm if input precision supports it.
Check 0<o<12 as required by a nondegenerate right triangle.
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not present 7.716 cm as a verified exact geometry measurement.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate angle from a leg ratio
WorkedExamples.Question: A right triangle has opposite leg 6 and adjacent leg 6 for reference angle θ. Estimate θ.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use matching legs and angle sum.
Steps: The legs are equal, so their opposite acute angles are equal.
Both acute angles total 90°, hence θ=45°.
A right-triangle ratio table should show ratio 1 near 45°.
WorkedExamples.Check: Here the equal-leg argument is exact, despite the table-based context.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recover a hypotenuse
WorkedExamples.Question: A right-triangle table gives adjacent/hypotenuse≈0.8 and adjacent leg 8 m. Estimate hypotenuse.
Steps: The exact result is contingent on how accurately 0.8 represents the underlying quotient.
WorkedExamples.Check: If 0.8 is a rounded table value, the answer should be reported as an estimate.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Naming ratios with memorized trigonometry vocabulary too early
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: This lesson's source deliberately develops descriptive quotients and table interpretation first.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Describe the legs and quotients here; formal names follow in Lesson 6.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a rounded quotient as if exact

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: estimate angles and missing sides from a measured right-triangle ratio table, before introducing formal cosine, sine and tangent names.
An acute reference angle in a nondegenerate right triangle determines side ratios; keep the calculator in degree mode.
Honest teacher-reviewed models and diagrams remain distinct from digitally checked numerical results.

Lessons.Title: Working with Trigonometric Ratios
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: name cosine, sine and tangent for an acute angle in a right triangle; use degree-mode calculations to solve missing sides and report reasonable precision.

The source intentionally introduces the names AFTER the ratio table built earlier; explain relationship cos, sin, tan instead of beginning with a mnemonic. The calculator may display irrelevant excess decimals.

Teacher rubric (0–8): four human-scored 0/1/2 criteria evaluate named cosine/sine/tangent from prior source tables, degree-mode and precision correctness, two source self-contained 12/71-degree triangle solutions with complementary-angle verification, and eight source Practice items including justified figure-dependent limitations.

First-party Edulytiks worked reasoning aligned to Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 4, CC BY 4.0. Publisher graphics, protected assessment answers and logos are not reproduced.

Source 6.1 This Time with Strategies (5 min): return to the earlier source picture asking for unknown z, first estimate with the existing right-triangle ratio table and compare methods before introducing new names. Numeric given for 6.1 is in a figure not fully represented in public text; do not invent its answer. Source 6.2 identifies a separate diagram with 50-degree angle, adjacent3 and hypotenuse z, so z=3/cos(50deg) about4.67 units.

Source 6.2 New Names Same Ratios (15 min): NOW name the three earlier columns IN SOURCE ORDER: cosine=adjacent/hypotenuse, sine=opposite/hypotenuse, tangent=opposite/adjacent for an acute angle in a right triangle. Calculator must be in DEGREES, not radians, and cosine/sine/tangent are dimensionless. Compare source calculator 50-degree values cos .642788 sin .766044 tan1.191754 and 40-degree values cos .766044 sin .642788 tan .839100 to prior source table rounded to .643,.766,1.192 and .766,.643,.839. Treat 3/cos50 as exact expression and about4.7 as measurement-level estimate, not false exact decimal.

Source 6.3 Solve These Triangles (15 min): pair-share three figure-based x,y/missing-length questions whose numeric image annotations are not available as text, plus two self-contained original problems. Triangle XYZ has X90, Y12, XZ2cm (opposite Y), so YZ=hypotenuse=2/sin12 degrees about9.62cm and XY=2/tan12 about9.41cm; third angle Z78. Triangle KLM has K90, L71, LM20cm hypotenuse, so KL=20cos71 about6.51cm, KM=20sin71 about18.91cm and angle M19. Partners compare trig and Pythagoras, checking rounding effects.

Source 6.3 optional 80,85,89-degree table inquiry: as theta approaches 90 from below, cosine→0, sine→1, tangent→positive infinity. At exactly 90 a nondegenerate acute reference-angle RIGHT TRIANGLE model does not apply: tangent90 is undefined, NOT 0 or infinity as a finite number. The source asks students to conjecture from calculator values, not simply accept advanced domain conventions as memorized facts.

Source lesson synthesis END right triangle: source paired complementary angles35 and55 give cos35=d/n, sin35=e/n, tan35=e/d; cos55=e/n, sin55=d/n, tan55=d/e. If d=6 source obtains e about4.2 and n about7.3 (e=6*tan35 about4.201, n=6/cos35 about7.325). Explicitly map reference angle and denominator before choosing formula. Source student summary for 25 angle with adjacent7 gives c=7/cos25 about7.72 and opposite a=7tan25 about3.26; rounded3.3 and7.7 make 3.3²+7²≈7.7², not exact equality.

Source Practice P1-P8: P1 original diagram has legs4,9 and hyp sqrt97, but options A-E involve theta/beta whose pictured angle position is missing; option E 4²+9²=97 ALWAYS true, other choices require original diagram. P2 expressions for JH,GJ require given labelled picture, no fabricated expressions. P3 Andre legs9,12 and hyp15 are valid, Clare angle B20 BC≈14.1 works since BC=15cos20; BOTH correct. P4 5-12-13 triple, acute angles approx22.62 and67.38. P5 inverse ratio estimates: adj/hyp .966 angle15; opposite/hyp .469 angle28; adj/hyp .309 angle72; opposite/adj1.036 angle46. P6 source rows .573,.819,1.428 and .819,.573,.700 correspond complementary angles about55 and35 with swapped ratios. P7 30-60-90 missing legs source-image-dependent. P8 Elena's altitude-based right triangle proof uses a/x=c/a and b/y=c/b, hence a²=xc b²=yc and a²+b²=c(x+y)=c². Original source 6.4 Cool-down Solve That Triangle teacher-locked; first-party diagram and partner explanations human-scored.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cosine
KeyConcepts.Definition: Cosine θ is adjacent leg/hypotenuse for acute 0°<θ<90°.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sine
KeyConcepts.Definition: Sine θ is opposite leg/hypotenuse for acute θ.

KeyConcepts.Title: Tangent
KeyConcepts.Definition: Tangent θ is opposite leg/adjacent leg, with nonzero adjacent leg.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find hypotenuse using cosine
WorkedExamples.Question: A right triangle has an acute 60° angle and adjacent leg 5 cm. Find hypotenuse.
Steps: Check h>5 and the implied opposite leg is 5√3.
WorkedExamples.Check: Correct reference angle is 60°, not its 30° complement.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find opposite using sine
WorkedExamples.Question: For acute 30°, hypotenuse 14 m, find opposite leg.
Steps: Multiply by 14 to get o=7 m.
WorkedExamples.Check: Degree mode required for calculator sine; special values are exact.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find rise using tangent
WorkedExamples.Question: A right-triangle ramp rises at 45° over horizontal run 3 m. Find rise.
Steps: Check slope triangle has congruent legs.
WorkedExamples.Check: This is a geometry problem, not a safety/compliance determination.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Choosing cosine for the ratio opposite/adjacent
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The numerator and denominator do not match cosine's definition.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Mark θ and choose sine (opp/hyp), cosine (adj/hyp), or tangent (opp/adj).

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Entering degrees with calculator in radians mode
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The numerical ratio output becomes unrelated to the stated degree angle.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Set and document degree mode and round only after full calculation.

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: name cosine, sine and tangent for an acute angle in a right triangle; use degree-mode calculations to solve missing sides and report reasonable precision.
An acute reference angle in a nondegenerate right triangle determines side ratios; keep the calculator in degree mode.

Lessons.Title: Applying Ratios in Right Triangles
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: ask for sufficient missing triangle data, use sine/cosine/tangent to estimate heights, and explain uncertainty and contextual model conditions.
This source lesson uses an information-gap exchange and indirect measurement of large objects. The independent Edulytiks model asks for exact missing quantities instead of reproducing source cards.

Student evidence: produce a correctly labelled right triangle, write the ratio choice with a reason, carry units and verify plausible magnitude. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct model, angle/side correspondence, arithmetic and precision, and sound independent explanation. Authentic partner discussion and drawings require teacher scoring; numeric checks alone do not assess them.

First-party Edulytiks worked reasoning aligned to Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 4, CC BY 4.0. Publisher graphics, protected assessment answers and logos are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Information sufficiency
KeyConcepts.Definition: One acute angle and one nonzero side of a right triangle fixes all other side lengths.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Ask whether given side is opposite, adjacent or hypotenuse.

KeyConcepts.Title: Height model
KeyConcepts.Definition: For a level horizontal distance d and angle of elevation θ, vertical rise h=d tanθ.
KeyConcepts.Example: At θ=45°, d=25 m gives rise 25 m.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rounding impact
KeyConcepts.Definition: Approximated trigonometric quotients can cause larger absolute errors for large distances.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Carry calculator precision until final reporting and reflect input measurement accuracy.
KeyConcepts.Example: tan30°≈0.577, multiplied by 100 m gives rise≈57.7 m.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate height from elevation
WorkedExamples.Question: Observer eye height is 1.6 m, horizontal distance to tower 40 m, elevation θ=30°. Estimate total height.
Steps: The vertical rise above eye level is 40 tan30°=40/√3≈23.094 m.
Round to about 24.7 m under the given measurement precision.
WorkedExamples.Check: Requires the observer and tower base to be on the same horizontal level.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find missing ground distance
WorkedExamples.Question: A hypothetical pole top is 9 m above sight level and is seen at elevation 45°. Find horizontal distance.
Steps: Check both perpendicular legs are 9 m.
WorkedExamples.Check: Distance is not the hypotenuse; it lies along level ground.

WorkedExamples.Title: Ask for necessary data
WorkedExamples.Question: Only a 60° elevation angle to a tower is known. Can absolute height be found?
Steps: For horizontal run 1 m rise √3 m.
For run 10 m rise 10√3 m; both have the same angle.
Ask for ground distance and observer eye height (or an equivalent known side).
WorkedExamples.Answer: No unique absolute height without a length measurement.
WorkedExamples.Check: An angle constrains shape, not the linear scale.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying a triangle ratio without a right-triangle model
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The interpretation may be wrong for slopes, unlevel ground or curved paths.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw and label the right angle and make contextual assumptions explicit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Rounding intermediate tangent to one decimal on a long baseline
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Small ratio error may create a large absolute height error.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Retain precision until final answer and report input uncertainty.

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: ask for sufficient missing triangle data, use sine/cosine/tangent to estimate heights, and explain uncertainty and contextual model conditions.
An acute reference angle in a nondegenerate right triangle determines side ratios; keep the calculator in degree mode.
Honest teacher-reviewed models and diagrams remain distinct from digitally checked numerical results.

Lessons.Title: Sine and Cosine in the Same Right Triangle
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: prove the complementary-angle identity sinθ=cos(90°−θ) for acute right-triangle angles and use it to justify equal length solutions from differently labelled diagrams.
The official lesson explicitly asks students to draft, peer-edit and explain the complementary identity in words and diagrams. Human scoring must evaluate that proof, not a calculator equality.

Student evidence: produce a correctly labelled right triangle, write the ratio choice with a reason, carry units and verify plausible magnitude. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct model, angle/side correspondence, arithmetic and precision, and sound independent explanation. Authentic partner discussion and drawings require teacher scoring; numeric checks alone do not assess them.

First-party Edulytiks worked reasoning aligned to Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 4, CC BY 4.0. Publisher graphics, protected assessment answers and logos are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Complementary angles
KeyConcepts.Definition: The two acute angles of any nondegenerate right triangle sum to 90°.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If one is θ, the other is φ=90°−θ.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sine/cosine correspondence
KeyConcepts.Definition: A leg opposite θ is adjacent to φ in the same right triangle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Not a general negative-angle swap
KeyConcepts.Definition: The identity is tied to complementary angles in a right triangle, not any pair of angle inputs.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prove complementary identity
WorkedExamples.Question: For right triangle with acute θ and φ, prove sinθ=cosφ.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use side roles in the SAME triangle.
Steps: The leg opposite θ is the same leg adjacent to φ.
Both ratios use the same hypotenuse h>0.
WorkedExamples.Check: Proof does not rely on rounded calculator decimals.

WorkedExamples.Title: Apply special-angle identity
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute cos60° using sin30°.
WorkedExamples.Check: Exact radical relationships support the special angle value.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two seemingly different equations
WorkedExamples.Question: A right triangle has θ=41°, φ=49°, a leg length 7 opposite θ. Show two equivalent equations for hypotenuse h.
Steps: The same leg is adjacent to φ: cos49°=7/h.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both equations give the same positive hypotenuse.
WorkedExamples.Check: Calculator approximations may differ by final displayed digits only.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming the same leg is opposite both acute angles
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Opposite/adjacent labels swap between complementary reference angles.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Mark the target angle and physically identify its opposite leg.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a calculator identity as the sole proof
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A numerical display tests examples, not all possible acute angles.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Explain the common opposite/adjacent leg and common hypotenuse.

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: prove the complementary-angle identity sinθ=cos(90°−θ) for acute right-triangle angles and use it to justify equal length solutions from differently labelled diagrams.
An acute reference angle in a nondegenerate right triangle determines side ratios; keep the calculator in degree mode.
Honest teacher-reviewed models and diagrams remain distinct from digitally checked numerical results.
